analysis.one_liner: Lets workers choose paid time off instead of cash overtime and lets employers shift up to 10 hours between weeks without overtime pay.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in March 2001, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let private-sector workers take 1.5 hours of paid time off instead of cash for each overtime hour worked, if they agreed in writing and could not be forced. It also would have let employers set two-week schedules, moving up to 10 hours from one week to the other, so a 50-hour week would not trigger overtime pay. It added protections: written agreements, cash-out of unused time, bankruptcy priority for owed comp time, penalties for coercion, and a five-year sunset.
analysis.who_benefits: Two groups: hourly workers who would rather have extra time off than extra cash, and employers who gain scheduling flexibility, can spread long hours across two weeks without paying the overtime premium, and can pay for overtime hours with time instead of money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Some hourly workers and their employers

how_it_helps.text: Workers could opt to receive one and one-half hours of paid time off for each overtime hour instead of the cash overtime premium, with written, voluntary agreements required and coercion prohibited on penalty of double damages [S3].

Employers could set up biweekly schedules of up to 80 hours over two weeks, shifting up to 10 hours into one week, so a 50-hour first week would not automatically earn overtime pay — flexible for workers with uneven family demands and cheaper for employers [S3].

Unused accrued comp time would have to be paid out in cash at the higher of the rate when earned or the final rate, including at termination, and would rank as a priority claim if the employer went bankrupt [S3].
The bill applied the same options to congressional employees under the Congressional Accountability Act, and the whole act would have expired five years after passage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who rely on cash overtime for their household budget, since employers could offer time off instead; and the overtime premium itself, whose deterrent against scheduling very long weeks is weakened by the biweekly option.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers counting on cash overtime pay

drawbacks.text: A worker under financial pressure may accept comp time instead of cash even when they cannot truly afford it, and the bill's own cash-flow logic — the employer holds the money and the worker holds a promise of future time — shifts risk from employer to employee; the annual cash-out requirement limits but does not eliminate this [S3].

The biweekly program would let an employer schedule a 50-hour week with no overtime premium at all, as long as the two-week total stayed at 80 hours, which weakens the overtime law's core incentive to cap long hours [S3].
The bill's protections against coercion rely on workers proving they were pressured, which in practice is difficult in non-union workplaces where a single agreement governs the relationship [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real trade here, not a simple one. Some workers with uneven schedules genuinely value an hour and a half of time off more than an hour and a half of pay, and the bill built in unusually strong safeguards: voluntary written agreements, cash-out at the higher pay rate, bankruptcy priority, and anti-coercion penalties. But the cash overtime premium is what makes 60-hour weeks expensive for employers, and both the comp-time swap and the 10-hour biweekly shift chip away at that price signal. On balance the bill helps a subset of workers while modestly eroding a wage protection that benefits hourly workers as a class.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg introduced the Workplace Flexibility Act on March 27, 2001, with Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison among its supporters [S1][S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers whose household budgets depend on cash overtime kept the existing guarantee untouched, since the bill never became law; employers did not gain the added scheduling flexibility it would have allowed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers whose paychecks rely on overtime

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded support was Republican — the sponsor and three Republican cosponsors out of 49 Senate Republicans — and there were no votes or recorded Democratic positions to show how the fight would have split.

industries.industry: Hourly-wage employers (retail, food service, manufacturing, services)
industries.note: The bill would have let these employers pay overtime hours with time off instead of cash and schedule 50-hour weeks without paying the overtime premium, lowering labor costs. The gain comes directly from the paycheck flexibility and cash overtime that hourly workers would give up, though voluntary-consent and cash-out rules soften the shift [S3].
